blocks.html: Internship Overview

After working at two startups, my curiosity about larger companies' design approaches led me to join Shure as a UX design intern on their general design team, where I worked on everything from design system maintenance to product redesigns.

As a musician and an avid user of Shure's microphones, I was fascinated by Shure's focus on audio. I was lucky to have amazing supervisors, who allowed me to go beyond the scope of my assigned task and explore my areas of interest, in the form of various smaller projects. <mark>Overall, this internship was a perfect introduction to audio-specific UX design, blending my passions for design and music.</mark>
In this case study, I discuss <mark>two of the projects I worked on</mark>:

PRISM 3 COMPONENTS -
Created 15 new components for Shure's design systemBEGINNER WORKFLOW -
Simplified equipment error handling for beginners
Outdated Components

<mark>Prism 2</mark> (Shure's previous design system) lacked several audio-specific components, and needed a revamp. Designers had several requests for missing components, and had to create them on the go, often <mark>losing up to 20-30% of design time on manual adjustments</mark>.
Customizable components, based on designers' requests.
I added <mark>15 new components to Prism 3</mark>, tailored to designers' needs, with enhanced customization through variants and instance swaps. <mark>All were approved for publishing.</mark>
Evaluating old components.
One of the components I created was a <mark>segmented control</mark>, which appeared in Prism 2 as a tabs component.
Segmented controls are a set of mutually exclusive options, presented horizontally.
Some of the <mark>problems</mark> that come with only having a tabs component are:

items: <mark>No distinction</mark> between general and specific navigation
<mark>Slows down workflows</mark> that require quick contextual switching
<mark>Users lose context</mark> when switching between tabs for related tasks.

blocks.html: How did other products use this component?
I explored the ways in which <mark>segmented controls</mark> were used in other products, to create a new and improved component.
Research Insights

items: Commonly used <mark>hover, selected, and focus states</mark>
Options differed in shape from standard buttons and were often <mark>visually connected</mark>

blocks.html: Audio-specific components were more complex.

To design components like <mark>audio meters</mark> and <mark>gain faders</mark>, I needed a deeper understanding of details like peak-indicator animation and decibel scales. <mark>I interviewed 3 designers</mark> who worked on relevant software to gain insights into their use of these components.
Interview Insights

items: Some components required <mark>manual adjustments</mark> due to spacing constraints or unique use cases.
Prism 2 over-relied on <mark>Material Design</mark>, which did not accommodate for audio-specific components.
Inconsistent components = <mark>visual inconsistencies</mark> across different products
The main use cases were <mark>horizontal and vertical input channels</mark>

blocks.html: How can we make the components more efficient to use, and save designers' time?
Opportunity Areas

items: Make <mark>component variations</mark>, reducing the need to detach instances
Create <mark>audio-specific components</mark>, tailored to designers' needs

blocks.html: Components should reference each other.

Even with lower-level components like <mark>segmented control</mark>, we tried to stay inspired by other components. For example, the design is highly influenced by the default and disabled state of standard buttons.
A lot of the low-level components like standard buttons were built on Material Design guidelines, which I had to familiarize myself with.

blocks.html: Audio-specific components needed more variation.

The goal was to <mark>reduce the need for manual adjustments</mark>. With the most common design scenario being vertical and horizontal channel strips, I began by creating <mark>vertical and horizontal scales</mark>.

In those scales, I utilized <mark>instance swaps</mark> to allow designers to hide/show right/left scales and numbers, switch between scales (decibel/log), and toggle between component types (meter/fader), as shown above.
Audio Meters & Faders
I interviewed designers to understand the way audio meter animations work, specifically the behavior of the Peak Indicator (the red mark), which showcases maximum loudness.
15 published components.
By the end of the internship, I created over <mark>15 components</mark>, which were approved for publishing.

blocks.html: Customizable Fader / Meter Component
I made it into Designer 6 :)

Although there is no concrete data on the time saved by designers using the new components, many of them—including the <mark>icon buttons</mark>, <mark>standard buttons</mark>, <mark>layouts</mark>, <mark>text inputs</mark>, the <mark>two-option segmented control</mark> I advocated for, and more—were included in <mark>Designer 6</mark>, released in <mark>February 2024</mark>.
What I learned from this project.

I learned a lot about <mark>specific Figma functions</mark> and <mark>components</mark>, from instance swaps, to nested instances, and more. I also got to learn about the <mark>format and organization of design systems</mark>, especially in the context of larger companies. This helped me understand how to utilize design systems in my designs correctly moving forward.

The main challenge was <mark>navigating the learning curve of Shure's organization of Prism 2</mark> and my initial inexperience with Figma's component functionalities. I owe a huge thank you to my supervisors, Christina and Anna, who were always available to answer my questions.
Wireless Workbench is too technical for beginners.
For inexperienced users, <mark>the current success rate of the error handling process is 30%</mark>. I was tasked with creating a more intuitive error-handling workflow.
User segmentation.

Providing users with <mark>tailored interfaces based on their experience</mark> with audio equipment,<mark> minimizing on-screen information</mark> to essentials, and <mark>automating error handling</mark> as much as possible.

items: <mark>Visual layout issues</mark> - small font, distracting background, confusing hierarchy

blocks.html: How can I help beginners take the first step towards fixing the devices?
Opportunity Areas
Errors needed to be straightforward.

Instead of each card representing multiple devices, <mark>the new card represents a single device</mark>, with a <mark>red border, showing an error</mark>. I replaced the red checkmark with an "error" icon for clarity.

blocks.caption: equipment error state iterations old vs new

blocks.html: I removed unnecessary information.

<mark>Users simply needed to see the malfunctioning devices.</mark> Thus, I hid information such as location-based optimization, and the wireless spectrum forecast. I also moved the 'getting started' section down in the hierarchy, since it is not relevant when the user is in a crisis.

I made sure to <mark>showcase all of the individual devices</mark>, and provide more visibility regarding their amount. <mark>I made the sections collapsable</mark>, with functioning devices not showing by default.
Clear instructions & visuals.

I proposed giving users clear visual steps when it comes to handling different errors. <mark>The instructions should be simple enough to follow without understanding the error types</mark>, and will appear as popups once a user clicks on a CTA.

blocks.html: What I learned from this project.

This project taught me that <mark>simplicity wins</mark>, especially in stressful situations. The main thing that helped me with creating the home screen was taking the users' mental state into account, and prioritizing their main concern - identifying which devices are malfunctioning, and taking the first step to fix them.
<mark>The main challenge was leaving my own bias and knowledge</mark> regarding audio and microphones behind, and "pretending" to be a complete beginner when designing.
First time at a big company.
Leave personal bias behind.
I observed professionals conducting user testing sessions and noticed that instead of correcting confused users or over-explaining their intentions they asked them to reflect on their decisions.
Users' emotional state is important.

Envisioning the users' emotional state while interacting with your design is critical to creating a good product. It was interesting to see just how important it is especially in the case of error-handling.
It takes a lot of people to make things work.
It was amazing to see how many different people with different strengths comprised the design team. I constantly felt inspired by my supervisors' visual design and research techniques.
Everything is a question away.

By reaching out to fellow designers and offering to help, I was able to explore additional audio-focused mini projects, and thus leveraged my background as a musician, utilizing this opportunity to the fullest.
